claim: The HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycoprotein binds to host cell receptors to mediate membrane fusion.
source: The HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycoprotein trimer, a trimer of gp120-gp41 heterodimers, is the infectious machinery that targets host cell receptors CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4 to mediate fusion between the viral and host membranes (Wyatt and Sodroski, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wyatt and Sodroski, 1998.

claim: The prefusion Env trimer is stabilized by V1V2 loops that interact at the trimer apex.
source: The prefusion Env trimer is stabilized by V1V2 loops that interact at the trimer apex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is consistent with structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) against V1V2 loops, exemplified by PG9, bind asymmetrically as a single Fab to the apex of the symmetric Env trimer using a protruding CDRH3 to penetrate the Env glycan shield.
source: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) against V1V2 loops, exemplified by PG9, bind asymmetrically as a single Fab to the apex of the symmetric Env trimer using a protruding CDRH3 to penetrate the Env glycan shield.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural studies described in the manuscript.

claim: BG1 is a new bNAb that binds with two Fabs per Env trimer using a compact CDRH3.
source: Here we characterized a distinct mode of V1V2 epitope recognition by the new bNAb BG1 in which two Fabs bind asymmetrically per Env trimer using a compact CDRH3.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the BG1-Env complex was solved at 6.2 Å resolution.
source: Comparisons between cryo-EM structures of Env trimer complexed with BG1 (6.2 Å resolution) and PG9 (11.5 Å resolution) revealed a new V1V2-targeting strategy by BG1.
evidence: The resolution is stated in the abstract and supported by the cryo-EM data collection and processing described in the methods.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the PG9-Env complex was solved at 11.5 Å resolution.
source: Comparisons between cryo-EM structures of Env trimer complexed with BG1 (6.2 Å resolution) and PG9 (11.5 Å resolution) revealed a new V1V2-targeting strategy by BG1.
evidence: The resolution is stated in the abstract and supported by the cryo-EM data collection and processing described in the methods.

claim: Env trimer is the sole target of neutralizing antibodies that prevent infection of host cells.
source: As the only viral protein on the surface of HIV-1 virions, Env trimer is the sole target of neutralizing antibodies that prevent infection of host cells (McCoy and Burton, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCoy and Burton, 2017.

claim: Most antibodies produced by an infected host are non-neutralizing or exhibit strain-specific neutralization.
source: Although an infected host produces antibodies against HIV-1 Env, most are non-neutralizing or exhibit strain-specific neutralization that is ineffective in the face of HIV's ability to create resistant variants through rapid mutation (McCoy and Burton, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCoy and Burton, 2017.

claim: Only a subset of HIV-1–infected individuals produce potent and broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs).
source: Only a subset of HIV-1–infected individuals produce potent and broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) (Klein et al., 2013; Landais et al., 2016), which can protect against and suppress infection in animal models (Klein et al., 2012; Barouch et al., 2013; Shingai et al., 2013) and exhibit antiviral activity in human clinical trials (Caskey et al., 2015, 2017; Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Klein et al., 2013; Landais et al., 2016; Klein et al., 2012; Barouch et al., 2013; Shingai et al., 2013; Caskey et al., 2015, 2017; Lynch et al., 2015.

claim: HIV-1 bNAbs can protect against and suppress infection in animal models.
source: Only a subset of HIV-1–infected individuals produce potent and broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) (Klein et al., 2013; Landais et al., 2016), which can protect against and suppress infection in animal models (Klein et al., 2012; Barouch et al., 2013; Shingai et al., 2013) and exhibit antiviral activity in human clinical trials (Caskey et al., 2015, 2017; Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klein et al., 2012; Barouch et al., 2013; Shingai et al., 2013.

claim: HIV-1 bNAbs exhibit antiviral activity in human clinical trials.
source: Only a subset of HIV-1–infected individuals produce potent and broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) (Klein et al., 2013; Landais et al., 2016), which can protect against and suppress infection in animal models (Klein et al., 2012; Barouch et al., 2013; Shingai et al., 2013) and exhibit antiviral activity in human clinical trials (Caskey et al., 2015, 2017; Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caskey et al., 2015, 2017; Lynch et al., 2015.

claim: HIV-1 bNAbs usually take 1–3 years to develop.
source: First, unlike most humoral immune responses, bNAbs usually take 1–3 years to develop (Klein et al., 2013; Landais et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klein et al., 2013; Landais et al., 2016.

claim: Nearly all HIV-1 bNAbs exhibit high levels of somatic mutation.
source: Second, nearly all HIV-1 bNAbs exhibit high levels of somatic mutation, and many of these antibodies include long heavy chain complementarity determining region 3 (CDRH3) loops (West et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to West et al., 2014.

claim: Many HIV-1 bNAbs include long heavy chain complementarity determining region 3 (CDRH3) loops.
source: Second, nearly all HIV-1 bNAbs exhibit high levels of somatic mutation, and many of these antibodies include long heavy chain complementarity determining region 3 (CDRH3) loops (West et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to West et al., 2014.

claim: The unusual features of HIV-1 bNAbs appear to be a significant barrier to eliciting such antibodies by immunization.
source: These unusual features appear to be a significant barrier to eliciting such antibodies by immunization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unusual features of HIV-1 bNAbs described in the manuscript.

claim: HIV-1 bNAbs have been mapped to distinct epitopes on HIV-1 Env including the variable 1 and 2 (V1V2) and variable 3 (V3) loops, the CD4 binding site (CD4bs) on gp120, the gp120-gp41 interface, and regions of gp41 including the membrane-proximal external region and fusion peptide.
source: HIV-1 bNAbs have been mapped to distinct epitopes on HIV-1 Env including the variable 1 and 2 (V1V2) and variable 3 (V3) loops, the CD4 binding site (CD4bs) on gp120, the gp120-gp41 interface, and regions of gp41 including the membrane-proximal external region and fusion peptide (McCoy and Burton, 2017; Landais et al., 2016; West et al., 2014; Burton and Mascola, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McCoy and Burton, 2017; Landais et al., 2016; West et al., 2014; Burton and Mascola, 2015.

claim: The V1V2 region of gp120 undergoes large structural changes after binding to the primary receptor CD4.
source: The V1V2 epitope is of interest because this region of gp120 undergoes large structural changes after binding to the primary receptor CD4: the interaction between CD4 and the gp120 portion of Env trimer stabilizes an open Env conformation that can interact with a chemokine receptor to induce further conformational changes resulting in insertion of the fusion peptide on gp41 into the target cell membrane (Wyatt and Sodroski, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wyatt and Sodroski, 1998.

claim: Structures of soluble native-like Env trimers in the closed, prefusion state showed that the V1V2 regions from the three gp120s interact around the trimer axis of symmetry to form a top layer of the trimer that shields V3 and the coreceptor binding site.
source: Structures of soluble native-like Env trimers in the closed, prefusion state (Garces et al., 2015; Gristick et al., 2016; Julien et al., 2013a; Kong et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2015; Lyumkis et al., 2013; Pancera et al., 2014; Scharf et al., 2015; Stewart-Jones et al., 2016; Ward and Wilson, 2017) showed that the V1V2 regions from the three gp120s interact around the trimer axis of symmetry to form a top layer of the trimer that shields V3 and the coreceptor binding site.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Garces et al., 2015; Gristick et al., 2016; Julien et al., 2013a; Kong et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2015; Lyumkis et al., 2013; Pancera et al., 2014; Scharf et al., 2015; Stewart-Jones et al., 2016; Ward and Wilson, 2017.

claim: In the CD4-bound state, the gp120 protomers are separated from each other.
source: In the CD4-bound state, the gp120 protomers are separated from each other (Liu et al., 2008; Tran et al., 2012), and the V1V2 loops are displaced by ~40 Å from the trimer apex to interact with CD4 on the sides of the trimer (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2008; Tran et al., 2012.

claim: In the CD4-bound state, the V1V2 loops are displaced by ~40 Å from the trimer apex to interact with CD4 on the sides of the trimer.
source: In the CD4-bound state, the gp120 protomers are separated from each other (Liu et al., 2008; Tran et al., 2012), and the V1V2 loops are displaced by ~40 Å from the trimer apex to interact with CD4 on the sides of the trimer (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Crystal structures of monomeric V1V2 scaffolds bound to PG9 or to its PG16 relative revealed the V1V2 loop structure as a Greek key motif containing four β-strands.
source: Crystal structures of monomeric V1V2 scaffolds bound to PG9 or to its PG16 relative revealed the V1V2 loop structure as a Greek key motif containing four β-strands that was recognized by the V1V2 bNAbs largely through interactions in which a long CDRH3 from the Fab reached through the Env glycan shield to contact a protein epitope in the V2 loop (McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013.

claim: V1V2 bNAbs recognize the V1V2 loop largely through interactions in which a long CDRH3 from the Fab reached through the Env glycan shield to contact a protein epitope in the V2 loop.
source: Crystal structures of monomeric V1V2 scaffolds bound to PG9 or to its PG16 relative revealed the V1V2 loop structure as a Greek key motif containing four β-strands that was recognized by the V1V2 bNAbs largely through interactions in which a long CDRH3 from the Fab reached through the Env glycan shield to contact a protein epitope in the V2 loop (McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013.

claim: Only one PG9 bound per Env trimer, resulting in an asymmetric quaternary epitope at the Env apex.
source: The EM structure and complementary biophysical studies indicated that, unlike bNAbs in other epitope classes that bind symmetrically to Env trimers with three Fabs per trimer, only one PG9 bound per Env trimer, resulting in an asymmetric quaternary epitope at the Env apex (Julien et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Julien et al., 2013b.

claim: Recent cryo-EM structures of Env trimer complexes with the V1V2 bNAb PGT145 revealed one V1V2 Fab per Env trimer and details of quaternary contacts spanning the three gp120 protomers of Env.
source: Recent cryo-EM structures of Env trimer complexes with the V1V2 bNAb PGT145 also revealed one V1V2 Fab per Env trimer and details of quaternary contacts spanning the three gp120 protomers of Env (Liu et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2017.

claim: BG1 was isolated along with bNAbs targeting non-overlapping sites on Env from an HIV-1 controller who developed elite levels of HIV-1 neutralizing activity.
source: A new V1V2 bNAb, BG1, was isolated along with bNAbs targeting non-overlapping sites on Env from an HIV-1 controller who developed elite levels of HIV-1 neutralizing activity (Freund et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Freund et al., 2017.

claim: The BG1 CDRH3 length is 22 residues, which is shorter than CDRH3 loops in other V1V2 bNAbs.
source: The BG1 CDRH3 length, 22 residues, is shorter than CDRH3 loops in other V1V2 bNAbs (Figure 1A), but longer than typical human antibody CDRH3s for which the most common length is 14 residues (Swindells et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to Swindells et al., 2017.

claim: The most common length for typical human antibody CDRH3s is 14 residues.
source: The BG1 CDRH3 length, 22 residues, is shorter than CDRH3 loops in other V1V2 bNAbs (Figure 1A), but longer than typical human antibody CDRH3s for which the most common length is 14 residues (Swindells et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Swindells et al., 2017.

claim: A 2.0 Å crystal structure of unbound BG1 Fab revealed that the BG1 CDRH3 does not extend notably beyond the antigen-binding site surface.
source: A 2.0 Å crystal structure of unbound BG1 Fab (Figure 1B; Table 1) revealed that, in contrast to the protruding CDRH3s in other V1V2 bNAbs, the BG1 CDRH3 does not extend notably beyond the antigen-binding site surface (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data presented in Figure 1B, Figure 1C, and Table 1.

claim: The relatively compact CDRH3 of BG1 results from folding into an irregular structure whose conformation is stabilized by Tyr100CCDRH3 interactions with protein backbone atoms in CDRH1 and CDRH3 and by water-mediated H-bonds involving other residues.
source: The relatively compact CDRH3 of BG1 results from folding into an irregular structure whose conformation is stabilized by Tyr100CCDRH3 interactions with protein backbone atoms in CDRH1 and CDRH3 and by water-mediated H-bonds involving other residues (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: None of the four tyrosines within the BG1 CDRH3 or within other CDRs show electron density for a sulfate group.
source: None of the four tyrosines within the BG1 CDRH3 (Tyr100ACDRH3, Tyr100CCDRH3, Tyr100JCDRH3 and Tyr100LCDRH3) or within other CDRs show electron density for a sulfate group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the electron density data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CDRH3s of other V1V2 bNAbs form stable subdomains involving regions of two-stranded β-sheet.
source: By contrast, the CRH3s of other V1V2 bNAbs form stable subdomains involving regions of two-stranded β-sheet (Figure 1E), sometimes containing sulfated tyrosine sidechains (e.g., PG9's Tyr100GCDRH3 and Tyr100HCDRH3) that interact with basic residues within V1V2 (McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1E and citations to McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2017.

claim: The CDRH2 loop of BG1 is two residues longer than CDRH2s of other V1V2 bNAbs.
source: The CDRH2 loop of BG1 is two residues longer than CDRH2s of other V1V2 bNAbs (Figure 1A), and it extends further from the antigen-binding site than the CDRH2 loops of other V1V2 bNAbs. (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment in Figure 1A and the structural data in Figure 1E.

claim: The CDRH2 loop of BG1 extends further from the antigen-binding site than the CDRH2 loops of other V1V2 bNAbs.
source: The CDRH2 loop of BG1 is two residues longer than CDRH2s of other V1V2 bNAbs (Figure 1A), and it extends further from the antigen-binding site than the CDRH2 loops of other V1V2 bNAbs. (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data in Figure 1E.

claim: The combined effects of the relatively compact CDRH3 and protruding CDRH2 result in the BG1 antigen-binding site being more flat than the combining sites of other V1V1 bNAbs.
source: The combined effects of the relatively compact CDRH3 and protruding CDRH2 result in the BG1 antigen-binding site being more flat than the combining sites of other V1V1 bNAbs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data in Figure 1E.

claim: The BG1 CDRH2 includes a solvent-exposed tryptophan at position 52B.
source: The BG1 CDRH2 includes a solvent-exposed tryptophan at position 52B (Figure 1D) (lysine in the VH3-49*04 germline sequence from which BG1 is derived).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data in Figure 1D.

claim: Protein-protein interfaces often include surface-exposed hydrophobic residues.
source: Protein-protein interfaces often include surface-exposed hydrophobic residues (Dall'Acqua et al., 1996; Kelley and O'Connell, 1993; Wells and de Vos, 1996), suggesting that the long CDRH2, and this residue in particular, could be involved in the binding interface of BG1 with Env.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dall'Acqua et al., 1996; Kelley and O'Connell, 1993; Wells and de Vos, 1996.

claim: The long CDRH2 of BG1, and the tryptophan at position 52B in particular, could be involved in the binding interface of BG1 with Env.
source: Protein-protein interfaces often include surface-exposed hydrophobic residues (Dall'Acqua et al., 1996; Kelley and O'Connell, 1993; Wells and de Vos, 1996), suggesting that the long CDRH2, and this residue in particular, could be involved in the binding interface of BG1 with Env.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural features of BG1 and general knowledge about protein-protein interfaces.

claim: The molecular mass of the PG16 Fab–Env complex was consistent with a stoichiometry of 1 Fab per Env trimer.
source: The molecular mass of the PG16 Fab–Env complex was consistent with a stoichiometry of 1 Fab per Env trimer (Figure 2A), as previously shown by SEC-MALS and negative-stain EM for PG9 (Julien et al., 2013b), and the 8ANC195–Env complex stoichiometry was 3 Fabs per trimer (Figure 2A), consistent with crystal and EM structures of 8ANC195–BG505 Env complexes (Scharf et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the SEC-MALS data in Figure 2A and a citation to Julien et al., 2013b.

claim: The 8ANC195–Env complex stoichiometry was 3 Fabs per trimer.
source: The molecular mass of the PG16 Fab–Env complex was consistent with a stoichiometry of 1 Fab per Env trimer (Figure 2A), as previously shown by SEC-MALS and negative-stain EM for PG9 (Julien et al., 2013b), and the 8ANC195–Env complex stoichiometry was 3 Fabs per trimer (Figure 2A), consistent with crystal and EM structures of 8ANC195–BG505 Env complexes (Scharf et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the SEC-MALS data in Figure 2A and citations to Scharf et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016.

claim: The SEC-MALS profile for the BG1 Fab–Env complex indicated a stoichiometry of 2 Fabs per trimer.
source: By contrast, the SEC-MALS profile for the BG1 Fab–Env complex indicated a stoichiometry of 2 Fabs per trimer (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the SEC-MALS data in Figure 2A.

claim: Negative-stain single particle EM reconstructions of BG1-Env-8ANC195, PG9-Env-8ANC195, and PG16-Env-8ANC195 complexes were obtained at resolutions between 27 Å and 32 Å.
source: Single-particle 3D reconstructions of these complexes at resolutions between 27 Å and 32 Å resolution (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) revealed three 8ANC195 Fabs bound to BG505 Env trimer in the expected positions at the gp120-gp41 interface (Scharf et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; Scharf et al., 2014) of each complex.
evidence: This is supported by the negative-stain EM data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BG1-Env-8ANC195 complex showed density for two BG1 Fabs per Env trimer.
source: The BG1-Env-8ANC195 complex showed density for two BG1 Fabs per Env trimer, while the PG9-Env-8ANC195 and PG16-Env-8ANC195 complexes each showed density for one Fab per trimer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the negative-stain EM data in Figure 2B.

claim: The PG9-Env-8ANC195 and PG16-Env-8ANC195 complexes each showed density for one Fab per trimer.
source: The BG1-Env-8ANC195 complex showed density for two BG1 Fabs per Env trimer, while the PG9-Env-8ANC195 and PG16-Env-8ANC195 complexes each showed density for one Fab per trimer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the negative-stain EM data in Figure 2B.

claim: The positions of the single PG9 and PG16 Fabs at the apex of Env trimer were similar to each other and to a previous negative-stain PG9-Env structure.
source: The positions of the single PG9 and PG16 Fabs at the apex of Env trimer were similar to each other and to a previous negative-stain PG9-Env structure (Julien et al., 2013b), whereas the BG1 Fabs bound Env in an orientation distinct from the orientations of PGT145 (Liu et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2017), PG9, and PG16 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the negative-stain EM data in Figure 2C and a citation to Julien et al., 2013b.

claim: The BG1 Fabs bound Env in an orientation distinct from the orientations of PGT145, PG9, and PG16.
source: The positions of the single PG9 and PG16 Fabs at the apex of Env trimer were similar to each other and to a previous negative-stain PG9-Env structure (Julien et al., 2013b), whereas the BG1 Fabs bound Env in an orientation distinct from the orientations of PGT145 (Liu et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2017), PG9, and PG16 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the negative-stain EM data in Figure 2C and citations to Liu et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2017.

claim: The geometric mean MNR for BG1 was 8.4, sdgeom (geometric standard deviation) = 2.4.
source: We found that the geometric mean MNR for BG1 was 8.4, sdgeom (geometric standard deviation) = 2.4 (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the neutralization data in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: The mean MNRs for PG9, PG16, VRC01, and 3BNC60 were comparable to the mean MNR for BG1.
source: The mean MNRs for these bNAbs were comparable to the mean MNR for BG1 (PG9: 6.0, sdgeom = 4.1; PG16: 10.3, sdgeom = 3.4; VRC01: 4.8, sdgeom = 3.1; 3BNC60: 8.1, sdgeom = 3.2) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the neutralization data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mean MNR for a 3BNC60-based reagent that exhibited neutralization potency increases suggestive of intra-spike crosslinking was 141, sdgeom = 2.1.
source: By contrast, the mean MNR for a 3BNC60-based reagent that exhibited neutralization potency increases suggestive of intra-spike crosslinking (a bivalent form of 3BNC60 in which two 3BNC60 Fabs were joined by a double-stranded DNA linker [Galimidi et al., 2015]) was 141, sdgeom = 2.1.
evidence: This is supported by the neutralization data and a citation to Galimidi et al., 2015.

claim: BG1 IgG does not bind bivalently to Env trimers during neutralization.
source: These results suggest that, like other natural HIV-1 bNAbs, BG1 IgG does not bind bivalently to Env trimers during neutralization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MNR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A single-particle reconstruction of a BG1-Env-8ANC195 complex with two BG1 Fabs per Env trimer was obtained at a resolution of ~6.2 Å.
source: A single-particle reconstruction of a BG1-Env-8ANC195 complex with two BG1 Fabs per Env trimer was obtained at a resolution of ~6.2 Å (calculated using the 0.143 gold-standard Fourier shell coefficient cutoff criterion) (Scheres and Chen, 2012) (Figure 3;Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2; Video 1; Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data in Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2, Video 1, and Table 2, and a citation to Scheres and Chen, 2012.

claim: Within the limits of the resolution of the cryo-EM structure, the CDRH3 and CDRH2 loops of BG1_A and BG1_B adopted the same conformation as their counterparts in the unbound BG1 crystal structure.
source: Within the limits of the resolution of the cryo-EM structure, the CDRH3 and CDRH2 loops of BG1_A and BG1_B adopted the same conformation as their counterparts in the unbound BG1 crystal structure (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The relatively compact CDRH3 loop observed in the unbound BG1 crystal structure was maintained in the 2:1 BG1-Env structure.
source: In particular, the relatively compact CDRH3 loop observed in the unbound BG1 crystal structure (Figure 1E) was maintained in the 2:1 BG1-Env structure (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data in Figure 3C and the crystal structure data in Figure 1E.

claim: A 27 Å BG1-Env-8ANC195 complex with three BG1 Fabs per Env trimer (3:1 BG1-Env) was reconstructed from a minor subset of the total particles (<10%).
source: A 27 Å BG1-Env-8ANC195 complex with three BG1 Fabs per Env trimer (3:1 BG1-Env) was also reconstructed from a minor subset of the total particles (<10%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and coordinates were fit to the density by rigid body refinement (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: An 11.5 Å single-particle cryo-EM reconstruction of a PG9-Env-8ANC195 complex was solved.
source: We also solved an 11.5 Å single-particle cryo-EM reconstruction of a PG9-Env-8ANC195 complex (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The position of the single PG9 Fab on Env trimer in the cryo-EM structure was consistent with negative-stain structures reported here and previously.
source: The position of the single PG9 Fab on Env trimer in the cryo-EM structure was consistent with negative-stain structures reported here and previously (Julien et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and a citation to Julien et al., 2013b.

claim: The angle of approach of the PG9 Fab was different in the PG9-Env interaction predicted from modeling the PG9 Fab-monomeric V1V2 scaffold structure onto Env trimer versus in the PG9-Env EM structure.
source: The angle of approach of the PG9 Fab was different in the PG9-Env interaction predicted from modeling the PG9 Fab-monomeric V1V2 scaffold structure (McLellan et al., 2011) onto Env trimer versus in the PG9-Env EM structure (Figure 4B), likely due to accommodating glycans in a neighboring gp120 protomer in the trimeric Env that are not present in a monomeric V1V2 scaffold.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data in Figure 4B and a citation to McLellan et al., 2011.

claim: The difference in the angle of approach of the PG9 Fab in the PG9-Env EM structure versus the modeled structure is likely due to accommodating glycans in a neighboring gp120 protomer in the trimeric Env that are not present in a monomeric V1V2 scaffold.
source: The angle of approach of the PG9 Fab was different in the PG9-Env interaction predicted from modeling the PG9 Fab-monomeric V1V2 scaffold structure (McLellan et al., 2011) onto Env trimer versus in the PG9-Env EM structure (Figure 4B), likely due to accommodating glycans in a neighboring gp120 protomer in the trimeric Env that are not present in a monomeric V1V2 scaffold.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data in Figure 4B.

claim: Both BG1 and PG9 Fabs reached through the glycan shield between the Asn156gp120 and Asn160gp120 glycans to contact underlying V1V2 protein residues.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, the contact analysis predicted that both Fabs reached through the glycan shield between the Asn156gp120 and Asn160gp120 glycans to contact underlying V1V2 protein residues, but only PG9 made contacts with basic residues in a lysine-rich region of the V2 loop (Lys168gp120 and Lys169gp120).
evidence: This is supported by the contact analysis data in Figure 5A.

claim: Only PG9 made contacts with basic residues in a lysine-rich region of the V2 loop (Lys168gp120 and Lys169gp120).
source: As shown in Figure 5A, the contact analysis predicted that both Fabs reached through the glycan shield between the Asn156gp120 and Asn160gp120 glycans to contact underlying V1V2 protein residues, but only PG9 made contacts with basic residues in a lysine-rich region of the V2 loop (Lys168gp120 and Lys169gp120).
evidence: This is supported by the contact analysis data in Figure 5A.

claim: Substitution of Lys169gp120 reduces neutralization potency for PG9, but has only minor effects on BG1.
source: This prediction was validated by an analysis of in vitro neutralization data demonstrating that substitution of Lys169gp120 reduces neutralization potency for PG9, but has only minor effects on BG1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the neutralization data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Substitution of Thr132gp120 had more of an effect on BG1 neutralization than on PG9 neutralization.
source: Conversely, substitution of Thr132gp120 had more of an effect on BG1 neutralization than on PG9 neutralization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the neutralization data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Predicted protein-protein contacts were mediated by different CDR loops for BG1 versus PG9: CDRH2 for BG1 and CDRH3 for PG9.
source: Predicted protein-protein contacts were mediated by different CDR loops for BG1 versus PG9: CDRH2 for BG1 and CDRH3 for PG9.
evidence: This is supported by the contact analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Asn156gp120 glycan on both gp120_A and gp120_B was contacted by the BG1 CDRL1.
source: Contacts with Env glycans were also made differently for BG1 and PG9: The Asn156gp120 glycan on both gp120_A and gp120_B was contacted by the BG1 CDRL1, and the Asn160gp120 glycan was contacted on both gp120s by the CDRH2 and CDRH3 loops of BG1 and also by the CDRL3 in the case of BG1_B.
evidence: This is supported by the contact analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of a potential N-linked glycosylation site (PNGS) at position 130 of gp120 correlated with weaker BG1 neutralization.
source: The analysis revealed that the presence of a potential N-linked glycosylation site (PNGS) at position 130 of gp120 correlated with weaker BG1 neutralization (geometric mean IC50 = 25.7 µg/mL for strains including PNGS 130, versus 1.5 µg/mL for strains lacking PNGS 130) (Figure 5A; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the neutralization data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: PG9 was more potent on strains lacking PNGS 130 (geometric mean IC50 = 0.76 µg/mL for strains including PNGS 130, versus 0.24 µg/mL for strains lacking PNGS 130).
source: PG9 was also more potent on strains lacking PNGS 130 (geometric mean IC50 = 0.76 µg/mL for strains including PNGS 130, versus 0.24 µg/mL for strains lacking PNGS 130); however, the difference was larger for BG1 (17-fold for BG1 versus 3-fold for PG9).
evidence: This is supported by the neutralization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The difference in neutralization potency between strains with and without PNGS 130 was larger for BG1 (17-fold) than for PG9 (3-fold).
source: PG9 was also more potent on strains lacking PNGS 130 (geometric mean IC50 = 0.76 µg/mL for strains including PNGS 130, versus 0.24 µg/mL for strains lacking PNGS 130); however, the difference was larger for BG1 (17-fold for BG1 versus 3-fold for PG9).
evidence: This is supported by the neutralization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Residue 130 (Gln130gp120) lies directly within the protein region contacted by BG1, but is outside of the PG9 footprint.
source: This result is rationalized by the BG1 and PG9 epitopes on Env trimer: although residue 130 (Gln130gp120) is not part of a PNGS in the BG505 strain of Env in our structural studies, residue 130 lies directly within the protein region contacted by BG1, but is outside of the PG9 footprint (Figure 5A), suggesting that addition of an N-glycan at position 130 would more directly disrupt BG1 binding than PG9 binding.
evidence: This is supported by the epitope analysis data in Figure 5A.

claim: Addition of an N-glycan at position 130 would more directly disrupt BG1 binding than PG9 binding.

evidence: This is an inference based on the epitope analysis data in Figure 5A.

source: Predicted van der Waals clashes (red dots) demonstrated that a third BG1 Fab cannot be accommodated on the Env trimer structure without steric clashing (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling data in Figure 7C.

claim: Binding of three BG1 Fabs to Env trimer is possible, as indicated by the minor population of Env trimers with three BG1 Fabs in the 3:1 BG1-Env structure.
source: However, as indicated by the minor population of Env trimers with three BG1 Fabs in the 3:1 BG1-Env structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), binding of three Fabs is possible (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 7D.

claim: When three BG1 Fabs were bound, the Env trimer appeared more open than Env in the 2:1 BG1-Env structure.
source: When three Fabs were bound, the Env trimer appeared more open than Env in the 2:1 BG1-Env structure, as shown by a comparison of the BG1 Fab positions in the 2:1 and 3:1 BG1-Env structures (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison data in Figure 7E.

claim: The V1V2 epitope on HIV Env is targeted by bNAbs that make quaternary interactions that prevent opening of Env trimer to expose the V3 loop and coreceptor binding site, hence blocking conformational changes leading to fusion of the viral and host cell membranes.
source: The V1V2 epitope on HIV Env is targeted by bNAbs that make quaternary interactions that prevent opening of Env trimer to expose the V3 loop and coreceptor binding site, hence blocking conformational changes leading to fusion of the viral and host cell membranes (McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2015; Walker et al., 2011, 2009; Bonsignori et al., 2011; Doria-Rose et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2015; Walker et al., 2011, 2009; Bonsignori et al., 2011; Doria-Rose et al., 2014.

claim: Quaternary interactions visualized thus far for V1V2 bNAbs involve the binding of a single Fab to the apex of Env trimer.
source: Quaternary interactions visualized thus far for V1V2 bNAbs involve the binding of a single Fab to the apex of Env trimer (Julien et al., 2013b; Liu et al., 2017), but here we demonstrate that the stoichiometry of binding for the new V1V2 bNAb BG1 (Freund et al., 2017) is two Fabs per Env trimer, with a minor population of 3:1 BG1-Env complexes (Figures 2 and 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Julien et al., 2013b; Liu et al., 2017.

claim: The stoichiometry of binding for the new V1V2 bNAb BG1 is two Fabs per Env trimer, with a minor population of 3:1 BG1-Env complexes.
source: Quaternary interactions visualized thus far for V1V2 bNAbs involve the binding of a single Fab to the apex of Env trimer (Julien et al., 2013b; Liu et al., 2017), but here we demonstrate that the stoichiometry of binding for the new V1V2 bNAb BG1 (Freund et al., 2017) is two Fabs per Env trimer, with a minor population of 3:1 BG1-Env complexes (Figures 2 and 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figures 2 and 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and a citation to Freund et al., 2017.

claim: Epitopes for HIV-1 bNAbs are located in positions not predicted to allow simultaneous binding of both Fabs from an IgG to a single Env trimer.
source: We previously noted that epitopes for HIV-1 bNAbs are located in positions not predicted to allow simultaneous binding of both Fabs from an IgG to a single Env trimer (Klein and Bjorkman, 2010; Galimidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klein and Bjorkman, 2010; Galimidi et al., 2015.

claim: The two Fabs in IgG forms of V1V2 bNAbs that exhibit a 1 Fab per Env trimer stoichiometry cannot bind with avidity to an Env trimer.
source: By definition, the two Fabs in IgG forms of V1V2 bNAbs that exhibit a 1 Fab per Env trimer stoichiometry cannot bind with avidity to an Env trimer, and epitopes on HIV-1 Env that show a 3:1 Fab-Env stoichiometry are located in positions that are too far apart to allow simultaneous binding of both Fabs in an IgG to one Env (Klein and Bjorkman, 2010; Galimidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klein and Bjorkman, 2010; Galimidi et al., 2015.

claim: Epitopes on HIV-1 Env that show a 3:1 Fab-Env stoichiometry are located in positions that are too far apart to allow simultaneous binding of both Fabs in an IgG to one Env.
source: By definition, the two Fabs in IgG forms of V1V2 bNAbs that exhibit a 1 Fab per Env trimer stoichiometry cannot bind with avidity to an Env trimer, and epitopes on HIV-1 Env that show a 3:1 Fab-Env stoichiometry are located in positions that are too far apart to allow simultaneous binding of both Fabs in an IgG to one Env (Klein and Bjorkman, 2010; Galimidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klein and Bjorkman, 2010; Galimidi et al., 2015.

claim: Comparisons of neutralization potencies of BG1 Fab and IgG suggested that potential avidity effects for BG1 IgG were marginal.
source: However, comparisons of neutralization potencies of BG1 Fab and IgG suggested that, as found for other HIV-1 bNAbs, potential avidity effects for BG1 IgG were marginal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with no intra-spike crosslinking and only minimal inter-spike crosslinking or steric effects favoring an IgG over a Fab.
evidence: This is supported by the neutralization data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The apparent absence of intra-spike crosslinking for BG1 IgG can be rationalized by the angle of approach the Fabs adopted in the 2:1 BG1-Env structure: adjacent Fabs were oriented such that they point away from each so that the C-termini of the CH1 domains are too far apart (~85 Å) to be spanned by a natural IgG hinge region.
source: The apparent absence of intra-spike crosslinking for BG1 IgG can be rationalized by the angle of approach the Fabs adopted in the 2:1 BG1-Env structure: adjacent Fabs were oriented such that they point away from each so that the C-termini of the CH1 domains (to which the N-terminus of an IgG Fc would be attached) are too far apart (~85 Å) to be spanned by a natural IgG hinge region (e.g., the C-termini of the two Fabs in the crystal structure of intact IgG b12 (Saphire et al., 2001) (PDB 1HZH) are separated by ~18 Å).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and a citation to Saphire et al., 2001.

claim: HIV-1 Env has evolved to prevent bivalent binding by IgGs to Env trimer even when Fabs from two separate IgGs can bind to nearby epitopes.
source: Thus it appears that HIV-1 Env has evolved to prevent bivalent binding by IgGs to Env trimer even when Fabs from two separate IgGs can bind to nearby epitopes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and neutralization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Previously-characterized V1V2 bNAbs made primary interactions with Env that involved a long, negatively-charged CDRH3 that reached through the Env glycan shield to contact basic residues in the V2 loop.
source: Previously-characterized V1V2 bNAbs made primary interactions with Env that involved a long, negatively-charged CDRH3 that reached through the Env glycan shield to contact basic residues in the V2 loop (McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2015; Julien et al., 2013b; Liu et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2011, 2009; Bonsignori et al., 2011; Doria-Rose et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McLellan et al., 2011; Pancera et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2015; Julien et al., 2013b; Liu et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2011, 2009; Bonsignori et al., 2011; Doria-Rose et al., 2014.

claim: BG1's epitope shows glycan interactions dominating over protein interactions.
source: Although BG1 is directed against the same general region of Env, its epitope shows glycan interactions dominating over protein interactions, and the relatively long BG1 CDRH3 (Figure 1A) is folded into a compact structure (Figure 1D,E) that is used to make contacts with Env glycans rather than Env protein residues (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural and contact analysis data in Figure 1A, Figure 1D, Figure 1E, and Figure 5A.

claim: The role of reaching through the glycan shield to contact protein residues is taken by BG1's unusually long CDRH2.
source: The role of reaching through the glycan shield to contact protein residues is taken by BG1's unusually long CDRH2 (Figure 1E), resulting in a different epitope footprint on Env than seen for typical V1V2 bNAbs such as PG9 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural and contact analysis data in Figure 1E and Figure 5A.

claim: The 2:1 BG1-Env complex structure suggests a potential secondary interaction of BG1_B with the Asn160gp120 glycan on a neighboring subunit, gp120_A, using CDRL1.
source: The BG1_B Fab interacts not only with glycans on its primary subunit contact gp120_B; the complex structure also suggests a potential secondary interaction with the Asn160gp120 glycan on a neighboring subunit, gp120_A, using CDRL1 (Figure 6A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data in Figure 6A.

claim: The 2:1 BG1-Env structure does not predict secondary contacts for BG1_A.
source: By contrast to the BG1_B interactions with Env trimer, the 2:1 BG1-Env structure does not predict secondary contacts for BG1_A, a difference that may explain why BG1_A and BG1_B showed distinct angles of approach when we aligned the BG1_A–gp120_A and BG1_B–gp120_B complexes by superimposing the protein coordinates of the V1V2 regions (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data in Figure 7A.

claim: Differences in the interactions of BG1_A and BG1_B with Env trimer suggests a model for BG1 Fab binding to Env in which BG1_B binds first to the V1V2 epitope on gp120_B, its CDRL1 could then interact with the Asn160gp120 glycan from gp120_A, and then a second BG1 Fab, BG1_A, could recognize the Asn156gp120 and Asn160gp120 glycans from gp120_A.
source: Differences in the interactions of BG1_A and BG1_B with Env trimer suggests a model for BG1 Fab binding to Env (Figure 7F): If BG1_B binds first to the V1V2 epitope on gp120_B, its CDRL1 could then interact with the Asn160gp120 glycan from gp120_A. After that, a second BG1 Fab, BG1_A, could recognize the Asn156gp120 and Asn160gp120 glycans from gp120_A.
evidence: This is a model based on the structural data in Figure 7F.

claim: The intrinsic flexibility of N-linked glycans would allow BG1_A to capture an Env conformation in which the glycans are shifted away from the trimer 3-fold axis such that a potential clash with BG1_B is avoided.
source: In this model, the intrinsic flexibility of N-linked glycans would allow BG1_A to capture an Env conformation in which the glycans are shifted away from the trimer 3-fold axis such that a potential clash with BG1_B is avoided.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural data and the model presented in the manuscript.

evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and the model presented in the manuscript.

evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data in Figure 7D and 7E.

source: The low percentage of 3:1 BG1-Env complexes observed by cryo-EM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), despite incubation with a 9-fold molar excess of BG1 Fab (Materials and methods), suggests that formation of 3:1 BG1-Env complexes is rare.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cryo-EM data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Direct comparisons of BG1-Env and PG9-Env stoichiometry and cryo-EM structures illustrate the diversity of bNAb recognition of the V1V2 epitope at the apex of HIV-1 Env trimer.
source: Our direct comparisons of BG1-Env and PG9-Env stoichiometry and cryo-EM structures illustrate the diversity of bNAb recognition of the V1V2 epitope at the apex of HIV-1 Env trimer.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The results provide new information relevant to design of immunogens to raise antibodies against V1V2.
source: These results provide new information relevant to design of immunogens to raise antibodies against V1V2 (Escolano et al., 2017), an important target because the V1V2 loops are critical for maintaining the closed Env trimer structure in which the coreceptor binding site is shielded and conformational changes leading to fusion of the viral and host cell membranes are prevented.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript and a citation to Escolano et al., 2017.

claim: The V1V2 loops are critical for maintaining the closed Env trimer structure in which the coreceptor binding site is shielded and conformational changes leading to fusion of the viral and host cell membranes are prevented.

evidence: This is supported by the structural and functional data presented in the manuscript.
